definition: A bundle of code holding some data (its state) together with the actions (methods) that work on that data.
A template or blueprint for creating objects of one kind. Each object built from it is called an instance.
Keeping an object's inner details private so other code can only use it through its public actions.
Letting a new class start from an existing class, reusing its data and actions and adding its own.
Different kinds of objects answering the same request, such as "draw yourself", each in their own way.
An action an object can perform, usually reading or changing that object's own data.
Five rules of thumb for designing classes: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion.
A named, proven blueprint for solving a design problem that keeps recurring in software, adapted to each program.
Nickname for the four authors of the 1994 book Design Patterns, which cataloged 23 patterns.
A pattern that allows a class only one instance and makes it reachable from anywhere; often criticized for hurting testability.
A pattern where one piece of code decides which kind of object to create, so callers don't hard-code it.
A pattern where a publisher keeps a list of subscribers and notifies each one whenever something happens.
A pattern that puts interchangeable ways of doing one task behind a common interface, swappable while the program runs.
Handing an object the things it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of letting it create or look them up.
An independent line of work inside a program; several threads can run side by side and share the program's memory.
Actually running several tasks at the same instant, for example on different processor cores.
Starting slow work, like a network call, and doing other things until its result arrives instead of waiting idle.
A bug where the result depends on which task happens to run first, so it fails only sometimes.
Tasks stuck forever because each is waiting for something another one holds and won't release.
A token only one thread can hold at a time, used so only one thread touches shared data at once.
A single thread that runs small pieces of code one at a time as events, like finished network calls, arrive.
A lock in standard Python that lets only one thread run Python code at a time; now optional in newer builds.
A way of arranging data in a computer's memory so that the questions you ask most often are fast to answer.
A numbered row of items stored side by side, so you can jump straight to any position.
A structure that turns a key into a storage slot, so looking up a value by its exact key takes about the same time at any size.
Data kept in sorted, branching order, so each step of a search skips large parts of the rest.
A set of items (nodes) joined by connections (edges), used to answer questions about what links to what.
Shorthand for how an algorithm's time or memory grows as its input grows, such as O(1), O(log n) or O(n).
A tiny structure that says an item is definitely absent or probably present, trading a small error rate for much less memory.
The software that sits between programs and hardware, sharing the processor, memory and storage among many programs safely.
The core of an operating system, running with full control of the hardware and handling programs' requests.
One running copy of a program, with its own private memory and state, managed by the operating system.
A separate line of execution inside a process; threads in one process share its memory but each has its own stack.
A program's formal request to the kernel for something it cannot do itself, such as reading a file or sending data.
The technique that gives each process its own private view of memory, which the OS maps onto real memory chips.
A group of ordinary processes given their own isolated view of the system, using Linux namespaces, with resource limits from cgroups.
An agreed set of rules for how computers format, send and respond to messages.
The numeric address that identifies a device on a network so data can be delivered to it.
The Domain Name System, the Internet's address book that turns names like a website domain into IP addresses.
A transport protocol that delivers data reliably and in order, re-sending anything lost, after a short setup handshake.
A lightweight transport protocol that sends individual messages with no setup and no guarantee they arrive.
The request-and-response protocol browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data.
The time a message takes to travel from sender to receiver, often measured as a round trip.
How much data a connection can carry per second; more bandwidth does not shorten a single round trip.
A system that stores data so it survives crashes and lets many users query and change it safely.
The plan for a database's data: which tables exist, which columns they have and what each column may hold.
A question or instruction sent to a database, usually written in SQL, to read or change data.
A lookup structure, like a book's index, that lets a database find rows without scanning the whole table.
A group of database changes that all succeed together or all fail together, with no half-finished state visible.
Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability: the four guarantees a transactional database makes about its changes.
A log where a database records each change before applying it, so it can recover committed work after a crash.
A statement of something a system must do, such as letting users post a photo or reset a password.
A quality a system must have, such as speed, reliability or security, rather than a specific feature. Also called a quality attribute.
The agreed boundary of what will and will not be built in a given project or design.
A measurement of how well a service is doing, such as the share of requests that succeed or finish quickly.
A target value for an SLI, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over a month.
A promise to customers about service levels that carries a consequence, such as a refund or credit, when it is broken.
The amount of failure an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests at 99.9%, which teams can spend before slowing releases.
The value that a given share of measurements fall under; p99 latency is the time 99% of requests beat.
Quick, rough math using simple assumptions and known numbers to size a system before building it.
How many requests a system receives or handles each second; the standard way to express load.
The busiest moment of traffic, which can be many times the daily average and must be planned for.
The number of different people who use a product on a given day; a common starting point for estimates.
A factor of ten. Estimates aim to get this right, such as thousands versus millions, not exact digits.
Memorized approximate times for common operations, such as reading memory or crossing an ocean, used to estimate performance.
Deciding how many servers, how much storage and how much network capacity a system needs, including spare room.
A rule linking load and delay: items in a system equal arrival rate multiplied by average time each item spends inside.
A design decision where gaining one quality, such as speed, means giving up some of another, such as cost or freshness.
The property that every user sees the same, most recent data, no matter which copy they read from.
The property that a system keeps answering requests, even when some of its parts have failed.
A guarantee that copies of data may briefly differ but will all match once updates stop arriving.
How much total work a system completes per unit of time, such as requests handled per second.
An extension of CAP: during a network partition choose availability or consistency; otherwise choose lower latency or consistency.
Amazon's terms for decisions that are hard to reverse, deserving care, versus easy to reverse, deserving speed.
A short document recording one design decision, its context and its consequences, so later teams know why it was made.
An application whose features all live in one program that is built, shipped and run as a single unit.
A monolith whose code is split into clearly separated sections, such as orders and billing, with enforced rules about how they interact.
The package of software that gets put live in one go. A monolith has exactly one.
The full set of source code files that make up a program.
A model of three ways to scale software: copy the whole app, split it by function, or split the data.
Replacing an old system gradually by building new parts beside it and moving features over one at a time.
Slang for a codebase with no clear structure, where everything depends on everything else and changes break unrelated parts.
A small, independently deployed program that handles one business job and owns its own data.
An older, company-wide style for connecting business applications as reusable services, often through a central integration hub.
A layer of helper proxies placed beside each service to handle encryption, retries, routing and monitoring outside the application code.
A single front door that receives requests from apps and routes or combines them across the right backend services.
A sequence of small, separate database updates across services, with undo steps if a later step fails.
Amazon's term for a team small enough that two pizzas could feed it, owning one service end to end.
Services that are split apart but still must be deployed together, getting the downsides of both styles.
Running code where the cloud provider manages all servers and scaling, and you pay only for actual use.
A serverless model where you upload small functions that the platform runs automatically when a chosen event happens.
Amazon's serverless service that runs your functions in response to events and bills per request and run time.
The extra delay when the platform must set up a fresh environment before running a function for the first time.
When a function runs in an environment kept from an earlier request, so it starts faster.
The billing unit for function run time: the memory given to a function, in gigabytes, multiplied by seconds it ran.
Paying to keep a set number of function environments ready in advance so requests avoid cold starts.
Being tied to one cloud provider because your code depends on its services and moving would be costly.
A database that stores data in tables of rows and columns and links tables together through shared keys.
Structured Query Language, the standard language for adding, changing, deleting and finding data in relational databases.
A column whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table, like a customer number.
A column in one table that points to the primary key of another table, linking the two.
Combining rows from two tables that share a matching key into one result.
A group of database changes that either all succeed together or are all undone.
Designing tables so each fact is stored in one place, preventing contradictory copies of the same data.
A sorted lookup structure that lets the database find matching rows without reading the whole table.
"Not only SQL": databases that skip the classic relational table model for flexible shapes built to spread across many machines.
A database that saves each value under a unique key and fetches it back by that key, very fast.
A database that stores flexible, nested, JSON-like records; records in one collection need not share the same fields.
A database, like Cassandra, that groups rows under a partition key and spreads those groups across many servers.
A database that stores items as nodes and the connections between them as relationships, suited to networks.
The field whose hashed value decides which server stores a record, so reads can go straight there.
Copies of data may briefly disagree after a change, but they all catch up and match shortly after.
One key that receives so much traffic it overloads the server holding it, slowing everything nearby.
Storage that keeps whole files as objects in buckets, each found by a unique name and fetched over the web.
A stored file together with its metadata, kept and retrieved as one unit.
A container that holds objects in an object storage service such as Amazon S3.
An object's unique name inside its bucket; slashes in it only look like folders.
A price-and-speed tier for stored objects, from frequently accessed to cheap deep archive that takes hours to retrieve.
How unlikely a storage service is to lose your data; S3 is designed for eleven nines.
A central store of raw data of every kind, kept as-is and structured only when analyzed.
A time-limited link that lets someone download or upload one specific object without having their own cloud credentials.
A break in the network that splits servers into groups that cannot talk to each other.
Every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data.
Every request that reaches a working server eventually gets an answer, even if it might be out of date.
Copies of data may disagree for a while, but all end up the same once updates stop.
An extension of CAP: during a partition, trade availability for consistency; otherwise, trade speed (latency) for consistency.
The strict meaning of consistency in CAP: every operation appears to happen at one instant, in real-time order.
An answer based on an out-of-date copy of the data.
A full copy of a database kept on another machine.
One machine (the leader) accepts every change and passes it to copies (followers); older docs call this master-slave.
How far a follower copy trails behind the leader, during which it may show old data.
The leader waits for a copy to confirm each change before saying saved: safer, but slower.
The leader confirms changes immediately and copies them in the background: faster, but recent changes can be lost.
Promoting a follower to become the new leader when the old leader stops responding.
The minimum number of copies that must respond for a read or write to count.
Several copies accept changes at once and later reconcile any changes that clash.
One piece of a large dataset, stored on its own machine.
The field, such as a customer ID, that decides which shard each record lives on.
Splitting a database's records across several machines; another name for sharding.
Handling more load by buying a bigger machine instead of adding more machines.
A shard that receives far more traffic than the others, slowing things down.
A way to place data on a ring of machines so adding or removing one moves only a small share of data.
A formula that scrambles a key into a number, used to spread data evenly across shards.
Moving data between shards to even out storage and traffic as the system grows.
A set of agreed rules that lets one program ask another for data or actions.
One specific address where an API accepts a certain kind of request.
A unique label a client attaches to a request so the server can spot retries and avoid doing the work twice.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Splitting a long list of results into smaller pages that are fetched one at a time.
An opaque bookmark returned with a page of results that tells the server where the next page starts.
Labeling changes to an API so existing clients keep getting the old behavior until they choose to upgrade.
A change to an API, such as renaming or removing a field, that makes existing client code stop working.
An architectural style for web APIs where each piece of data has an address and is acted on with standard HTTP verbs.
Any named piece of information in a REST API, such as a customer or an order.
The unique web address that identifies a resource, like /orders/1.
The verb of a web request, such as GET to read, POST to create, or DELETE to remove.
Create, read, update, delete: the four basic actions on stored data.
A three-digit number in every HTTP response saying how the request went, like 200 OK or 404 Not Found.
The server keeps no memory of a client between requests; each request carries everything needed to answer it.
A REST principle where responses include links telling the client what it can do next.
An open-source framework from Google for fast, typed calls between services using compact binary messages over HTTP/2.
Calling a function that runs on another machine as if it were part of your own program.
Google's compact binary format for structured data, described in a contract file; like JSON but smaller and faster.
A plain text contract listing a service's methods and the shape of each message, used to generate code.
Generated client code that makes a remote call look like a local function call.
A newer version of the web's protocol that can carry many requests at once over a single connection.
The longest time a caller will wait for a reply before giving up on the call.
A gRPC call where the client, the server, or both send a sequence of messages instead of just one.
A lasting, two-way connection between a browser and a server that lets either side send messages at any time.
Asking a server over and over whether anything has changed.
A technique where the server holds a request open until it has news, then the client immediately asks again.
A one-way stream of updates from a server to a browser over a long-lived HTTP response, with automatic reconnection.
The opening web request in which browser and server agree to upgrade the connection to a WebSocket.
A server sending data to a client without the client asking for it first.
A small periodic message, such as a ping, that keeps a connection alive and checks the other side is still there.
A network of servers around the world that keeps copies of a website's files close to users so they load faster.
The website's own server that holds the original files; the CDN fetches from it when it lacks a copy.
A CDN location in a city near users that hands out cached copies of content. PoP stands for point of presence.
A hit means the edge already had the file and answered at once; a miss means it had to fetch it from the origin.
Files that are the same for every user, such as images, videos, style sheets and scripts, which CDNs cache well.
Telling a CDN to throw away a stored copy before it expires, so the next request fetches a fresh one.
A routing method where many data centers share one internet address and each user automatically reaches a nearby one.
A traffic director that sits in front of a group of servers and spreads incoming requests across them.
The simplest way to share work: each new request goes to the next server in turn, then back to the first.
A small test request sent on a timer to see whether a server works; failing servers stop receiving traffic.
A server that receives requests on behalf of other servers and forwards them; many load balancers work this way.
Handling more traffic by adding more machines side by side, instead of replacing one machine with a bigger one.
Keeping one user's requests on the same server for a whole visit, usually by means of a cookie.
One of the servers behind a load balancer that actually does the work for a request.
Layer 4 balancers route using only network addresses and ports; layer 7 balancers read the request itself, such as its web address.
A buffer that holds tasks sent by one part of a system until another part is ready to process them.
The part of a system that creates messages and puts them into a queue.
The part of a system that takes messages from a queue and does the work they describe.
The software that runs queues and delivers messages, such as Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ or Apache Kafka.
Publish/subscribe: a messaging pattern where one published message is delivered to every subscriber that wants it.
How long a received message stays hidden from other consumers before it reappears if not deleted.
A side queue that collects messages that failed processing too many times, so engineers can inspect them.
A guarantee that every message arrives, but some may arrive more than once, so consumers must handle duplicates.
Keeping spare copies of servers or data ready to take over when one breaks.
The share of time or requests a system works correctly, often written as "nines" like 99.99%.
The longest a program will wait for an answer from another service before giving up.
Retrying a failed request while waiting longer after each failure, for example doubling the wait each time.
Random variation added to retry wait times so many clients don't all retry at the same moment.
A safety switch that stops calling a failing service for a while and fails fast instead.
Dropping non-essential features during a failure so the core job keeps working.
A failure that spreads as overloaded parts push their work onto others, which then fail too.
The maximum number of requests a caller may make to a service in a given period of time.
Slowing down or rejecting a caller's requests once they reach their limit.
A usage allowance over a longer period, such as requests per day or per month.
The standard web error "Too Many Requests", telling a caller to slow down and try again later.
A limiter where each request spends a token and tokens refill steadily, allowing short bursts but capping the average rate.
A limiter that lets requests through at a fixed, steady pace, allowing no bursts.
A way of counting requests over the last fixed stretch of time from right now, avoiding bursts at window edges.
Deliberately rejecting less important requests when a service is overloaded, to keep critical ones working.
Proving to a system that you are who you claim to be, for example with a password, phone or fingerprint.
Logging in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a tap on your phone.
A password replacement made of two linked digital keys; the secret one stays on your device, so fake websites have nothing to steal.
Logging in once with a trusted provider, like Google or your employer, which then vouches for you to many other apps.
A standard that lets an app get limited, revocable access to your data elsewhere without ever learning your password.
A login standard built on OAuth that tells an app who you are, using a signed ID token from your identity provider.
A compact, signed text token carrying facts about a user, like their ID and expiry time, that servers can verify without a lookup.
A long random string your browser shows after login, acting like a key card so you don't re-enter your password.
Deciding what a known user or program is allowed to do, such as reading, editing or deleting a specific item.
Giving people roles like editor or admin, where each role comes with a fixed set of permissions.
Access rules that check facts about the user, the item and the situation, such as department, owner or time of day.
Access that follows links between people and things, such as owning a document or belonging to a shared folder's group.
Giving each person or program only the permissions its job truly needs, so a stolen account can do little damage.
A safety rule: if no policy explicitly allows an action, the system refuses it.
A bug that lets someone see or change data they shouldn't, like viewing another user's account by changing an ID.
Scrambling data with a secret key so only someone holding the right key can turn it back into readable form.
The Advanced Encryption Standard, the fast, widely used cipher where the same secret key locks and unlocks data.
Encryption using a matched key pair: a public key anyone can use to lock, and a private key only its owner uses to unlock.
TLS is the protocol that encrypts and verifies internet connections; HTTPS is ordinary web browsing carried over TLS.
Turning data into a fixed one-way fingerprint that cannot be reversed; used to store passwords safely and detect changes.
A digital document, signed by a trusted authority, proving that a public key really belongs to a particular website.
At rest protects stored data on disks and backups; in transit protects data while it travels across networks.
Encrypting data with its own key, then locking that key with a master key kept in a secure key service.
A timestamped record of one event that happened inside a program, such as a failed payment.
A label saying how serious a log event is, such as DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR.
A log written as labeled fields, often JSON, so tools can search, filter and count by each field.
Collecting logs from many machines into one central place where they can be searched together.
Elasticsearch, Logstash and Kibana: a popular toolkit to collect, store, search and chart logs.
An attack where crafted input adds fake lines to a log, hiding or forging what really happened.
A number about a system, such as requests per second, measured again and again over time.
A run of timestamped values for one measurement, which can be drawn as a line on a chart.
A screen of live charts built from metrics that shows a system's health at a glance.
An automatic message to an engineer that fires when a metric crosses a line someone set.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall; p99 latency is slower than 99% of requests.
Google's four key service metrics: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
How many distinct label combinations a metric has; each one is a separate series that costs memory.
A popular open-source system that pulls metrics from services, stores them and triggers alerts.
The full record of one request's path through all the services it touched.
One timed step of work inside a trace, such as a single database call.
The unique label shared by every span in one trace, used to stitch them together.
Passing the trace ID and related data along with each call from one service to the next.
Keeping only some traces, such as one in a hundred, to control storage and processing cost.
An open-source, vendor-neutral standard and toolkit for producing traces, metrics and logs.
An open-source distributed tracing system first built at Uber and now a CNCF project.
The big-picture plan of a system: its main parts, how they connect, and why each choice was made.
A short document written before coding that explains a planned system, its goals and the trade-offs behind it.
Something that could reasonably be a goal but that a design deliberately chooses not to do.
A one-to-two page note kept with the code that records one important design decision, its context and its consequences.
A simple way to draw software architecture at four zoom levels: system context, containers, components and code.
The section of a design doc listing other designs that were weighed and why they were rejected.
The part of a system that slows everything down first when traffic grows.
A detailed plan for one part of a system: its classes, the data they hold and how they interact.
A drawing that shows a program's classes, what each holds and does, and how they relate to each other.
Unified Modeling Language: a standard set of diagram types for describing software designs.
Five design principles for code that is easy to change, such as giving each class a single reason to change.
A proven, general solution to a common software design problem that you adapt rather than copy.
A fixed list of states something can be in, plus the rules for which moves between states are allowed.
A promise of what a piece of code can do, without saying how it does it.
A service that turns a long web address into a short code and redirects visitors from the code to the original.
Copying one new post into many followers' ready-made feeds at once, so reading a feed is fast.
Writing numbers using the 62 characters a-z, A-Z and 0-9, giving short codes that are safe in web addresses.
A 64-bit unique ID made from a timestamp, a machine number and a counter, so IDs sort roughly by creation time.
One slice of a database that gets far more traffic than the rest, slowing down the machines holding it.
Quick, rough math about users, requests and storage that tells you how big a design needs to be.
Describes a system that answers far more lookups than it stores new data.
A program that learned its behavior from example data instead of being written rule by rule.
Showing a model many examples so it learns patterns it can use on new cases.
Using a trained model to answer a new question or make a prediction.
A model slowly getting less accurate because the world has drifted away from the data it learned from.
The practices and tools for building, shipping, monitoring and retraining machine learning systems reliably.
Hidden long-term maintenance cost that builds up in AI systems from tangled data, glue code and missing monitoring.
Automatically retraining and redeploying a model on fresh data, a need unique to machine learning systems.
The result an organization wants from a project, stated in plain words, such as fewer fraud losses.
Anyone affected by or responsible for a system: users, sponsors, support staff, or people the system decides about.
A number that shows whether the business goal is being met, separate from the model's own accuracy scores.
A measurable stand-in for something you can't measure directly, like predicting likes as a stand-in for usefulness.
A false alarm versus a missed case; requirements should say which mistake hurts users more.
Precision is how many flagged items are truly correct; recall is how many true items get found. Raising one usually lowers the other.
The simple, often non-AI solution a model must clearly beat to be worth building and maintaining.
The part of an AI system that collects, cleans and turns raw data into features a model can learn from.
The part of an AI system that trains, tests and versions models before they are allowed into production.
The part of an AI system that runs the model to answer requests from apps and users.
The part of an AI system that watches data and answer quality and triggers fixes or retraining.
A shared library of model inputs that keeps history for training and fresh values for fast answers, so both match.
A catalog of trained model versions, how each was made, and which one is currently live.
Computing predictions ahead of time and storing them, versus computing each prediction the moment it is requested.
When a feature is computed differently during training than when serving live, so the model sees unfamiliar numbers.
Any system or place an AI system gets data from, such as databases, APIs, event streams, files or devices.
A central store that keeps structured and unstructured data in its original form, with structure applied only when the data is read.
A continuous flow of small records describing things that just happened, such as clicks, payments or sensor readings.
Copying every insert, update and delete from a database as it happens, by reading the database's own change log.
The correct answer attached to a training example, such as spam or not spam, added by people or software.
Moving data in large chunks on a schedule, such as a nightly copy of a database.
When a model sees different data values in production than it saw during training, which quietly hurts its accuracy.
A model trained on huge amounts of text that reads and writes language by predicting the next word or word fragment.
The branch of AI that works with human language, such as translation, summarizing or classifying text.
AI that understands images and video, for example naming objects in a photo or finding where they are.
A model that suggests items a person is likely to want next, such as videos, songs or products.
A model that predicts future numbers, like sales or website visits, from past values and patterns such as seasons.
The model design behind modern LLMs, which uses attention to weigh how every word relates to every other word.
When a language model produces fluent, confident text that is false.
Using a trained model to make a prediction or produce an answer for new input.
A chip with many cores that runs thousands of calculations at once, which makes it fast for AI math.
Google's custom chip designed specifically to speed up machine learning, rented through Google Cloud.
Renting computing power, storage and networking over the internet on demand, and releasing it when finished.
Running machines a company owns in its own building or data center, instead of renting from a cloud provider.
Spare cloud capacity rented at a discount that the provider can take back with a two-minute warning.
The delay when a paused service must start up its computers before it can answer a request.
Many GPU machines linked by a fast network so they can work together on one large training job.
A company's library of help articles and policies that a support assistant searches before answering.
A method where the AI first looks up relevant documents, then writes its answer based on what it found.
An automatic check around an AI model that blocks unsafe or off-topic messages and wrong answers.
Passing a customer conversation from the AI assistant to a human agent, usually for hard or risky cases.
The share of customer questions the assistant solves without any human help.
Letting an AI assistant call company systems, such as an order database, to look up or change real records.
Customer satisfaction score, usually collected with a short survey after a support conversation.
An attack where text from a user or a document tricks an AI into ignoring its instructions.
An automatic chain of steps that collects data, cleans it and delivers it where it is needed, again and again.
Extract, transform, load: copy data out of a source, clean and reshape it, then store it in its destination.
Extract, load, transform: store raw data in the destination first, then clean and reshape it there later.
Collecting data from apps, databases and devices into your system so it can be processed.
Handling data in large scheduled chunks, such as once every night.
Handling each piece of data the moment it arrives, instead of waiting to collect a big pile.
Automatic checks that incoming data has the expected types, ranges and patterns before a model uses it.
A stream processor's estimate of when all events for a time window have arrived, so it can publish results.
Showing a model many examples and adjusting its internal numbers until its mistakes shrink.
A setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate or how many passes over the data to make.
When a model memorizes its training examples and then does badly on new data it has not seen.
Reusing what a model learned on one problem to solve a similar problem with less data.
A short extra round of training that adapts a pre-trained model to your specific task or style.
A cheap fine-tuning method that freezes the original model and trains small add-on pieces instead of every weight.
Examples kept aside and never used in training, so they can fairly measure how the model will do in reality.
Logging every training run's settings, scores and resulting model so results can be compared and reproduced.
One measurable input a model uses to make a prediction, such as rides taken in the last seven days.
Rescaling numeric inputs onto similar ranges so no single large-valued feature dominates what the model learns.
Turning a category, such as a city, into a list of on/off slots with exactly one slot switched on.
A shared system that keeps feature history for training and the latest feature values for fast live predictions.
A mismatch between the data a model saw in training and the data it sees in live use, which hurts quality.
Building a model with information that will not exist at prediction time, which makes test scores look falsely good.
Using each feature's value exactly as it was at the moment of a past event, never a later value.
A new feature made by combining two or more features, letting simple models spot patterns that appear together.
A test that gives an AI system an input and uses grading rules to score its output.
Examples kept hidden from a model while it learns, used only to grade it at the end.
Of all the items a model flagged as positive, the share that really were positive.
Of all the truly positive items, the share the model managed to catch.
A single number that balances precision and recall, useful when one class is rare.
A live experiment that shows two versions to random groups of users and compares how each group behaves.
Using a strong language model to grade or compare another model's answers instead of a human reviewer.
When test examples, or copies of them, slip into training data and make a model look better than it is.
Running a trained model on new input to get a prediction or answer.
Running a model as a service that apps can call for predictions, quickly and reliably.
Answering each prediction request right away, as it arrives, from an always-on service.
Running a model over a large pile of data at once, with no live service, such as nightly scoring.
Giving a new version to a small share of users first, then widening it or rolling back.
Sending copies of real requests to a new model while users only see the old model's answers.
The delay while an idle, scaled-down service starts machines and loads the model before answering.
Grouping separate incoming requests on the server so the hardware processes them together, raising throughput.
A chip that does huge amounts of math at once, used to train and run AI models.
Many GPUs connected by very fast networks so they can work together on one job.
Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and trains on a different slice of the data.
Splitting one model across several GPUs because it is too big for a single chip's memory.
Giving each GPU a group of a model's layers, like stations on an assembly line.
A step where many machines combine their numbers, such as averaging, and all receive the same result.
Automatically adding or removing machines or copies of a service as demand rises and falls.
A saved snapshot of training progress, so a job can restart after a failure without starting over.
Continuously checking a live model's inputs, outputs and results so you notice when its answers quietly get worse.
When the data a model sees in real use gradually changes from the data it learned from.
When the link between inputs and the correct answer changes, so a model's learned lessons stop being true.
A mismatch between the data a model was trained on and the data it gets live, often caused by a bug.
The 'normal' data that live traffic is compared against, usually the training data or a past period of real traffic.
The real outcome, often known only later, used to check whether a model's prediction was right.
Recording each chatbot request, model call, tool call, cost and delay so you can explain why an answer went wrong.
Automating and monitoring every step of a model's life, from raw data and training to release and upkeep.
Continuous integration and delivery: automatically testing every change, then shipping it to users safely and repeatably.
Retraining a model automatically on a schedule, when new data arrives, or when its quality or input data drifts.
A scripted, repeatable series of steps, such as fetching data, checking it, training and evaluating, that produces a model.
A catalog of every model version, with notes on how each was made and labels marking which one is live.
Sending a small share of traffic to a new version first, so problems hit few users and can be rolled back.
Switching back to the previous model or software version quickly when a new release causes problems.
MLOps practices applied to large language model apps, including versioning prompts and testing them against evaluation sets.
Text that tricks an AI model into ignoring its intended instructions and doing something its builders did not want.
Prompt injection hidden inside content the AI reads, like a web page, document or email, rather than typed by the user.
Slipping harmful or misleading examples into the data a model learns from, so it learns the wrong behavior.
Personally identifiable information: details like names, phone numbers and email addresses that can identify a specific person.
An input changed slightly and deliberately so that a model gives a wrong answer with high confidence.
A mathematical guarantee that limits how much anyone can learn about one person from a dataset or its statistics.
Giving a system or AI assistant only the access it truly needs, so a mistake or trick does little harm.
Deliberately attacking your own AI system, the way a real attacker would, to find weaknesses before they are exploited.
A small chunk of text, roughly a short word, that AI providers count and charge for.
Having the provider reuse a long, repeated part of a prompt so later requests pay much less for it and answer faster.
Sending each request to a cheaper or stronger AI model depending on how hard the request looks.
Sending many non-urgent AI requests together to be finished within hours, in exchange for a lower price.
A spare cloud computer rented at a deep discount that the provider can take back with short notice.
Training a small student model to imitate a large teacher model, so it keeps much of the skill but costs less to run.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits so it needs less memory and fewer or cheaper chips.
The practice of engineering, finance and business teams sharing cloud and AI cost data to get the most value per dollar.
A backup model, provider or region that takes over a request when the main one fails.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt before trying a request again.
A small random delay added to retries so many clients do not retry at the same instant.
A switch in software that stops calling a failing service for a while and fails fast, giving it time to recover.
Offering a simpler or reduced service when something fails, instead of breaking completely.
An error some AI APIs return when the service is temporarily too busy across all users to handle a request.
The one person who leads and coordinates a team's response during an outage.
When an AI model keeps answering normally but its answers quietly get worse, without any visible errors.
An AI system systematically treating some groups of people worse than others.
A measurable rule for comparing how an AI treats different groups, such as equal approval rates or equal error rates.
Being able to show which factors drove an AI decision, so people can understand and question it.
A short document shipped with an AI model describing its intended use, how it was tested and its limits.
A person who can check, override or stop an AI system's decision.
The European Union's law that regulates AI systems according to their level of risk, with bans and strict rules for high-risk uses.
Under the EU AI Act, AI used in areas like hiring or credit scoring that must meet strict safety and oversight rules.
When a model infers a protected trait like gender from other data, such as words or schools, and treats people unfairly.
The most text, counted in tokens, that an AI model can handle in one request, including its own answer.
A small chunk of text, roughly a short word or part of one, that AI models read, count and charge by.
Standing instructions sent with every request that set the model's role, tone and rules.
Putting a few worked examples in the model's input so it copies their pattern, without retraining the model.
The drop in a model's accuracy at finding and using information as its input grows longer.
A provider feature that reuses the work of reading an identical start of a prompt, cutting cost and waiting time.
Replacing older parts of a long conversation with a short summary so the work can continue within the context window.
A list of numbers produced by an AI model that captures what a piece of text, image or audio means.
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the stored items whose vectors are closest to a query.
Finding results by meaning rather than by matching exact words, usually by comparing embeddings.
Search that finds almost-certainly-closest vectors by checking only part of the data, trading a little accuracy for big speed.
Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a popular ANN index that links vectors in layered graphs, searched from sparse top layers downward.
A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction; the usual way to compare text embeddings.
An open-source Postgres extension that stores vectors and runs exact or approximate similarity search beside regular data.
A compression method that splits vectors into pieces and stores short codes, letting billions of vectors fit in memory.
Searching your documents for relevant passages and giving them to an AI model so it answers from them.
Basing an AI answer on specific retrieved source text rather than on what the model memorized in training.
A confident AI answer that is false or made up.
Splitting long documents into short passages so each can be indexed and retrieved on its own.
Combining meaning-based vector search with keyword search, then merging both result lists into one ranking.
A classic keyword-ranking formula that scores documents by matching terms; strong at exact names and codes.
A way to merge ranked lists by summing 1/(rank + k) for each item, rewarding items ranked high in several lists.
A slower, more accurate second pass, often a cross-encoder model, that rescores top search results against the question.
Running a trained AI model to produce an answer, as opposed to training it.
Working notes a language model saves for every token so far, kept in GPU memory so it never recomputes them.
The two phases of answering: prefill reads the whole prompt at once; decode writes the answer one token at a time.
Serving many requests together where finished ones leave and new ones join at every step, so the GPU never sits idle.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, to save memory and speed it up.
A small fast model drafts the next few tokens and the big model checks them all at once, keeping identical output.
How long a user waits before the first word of an AI answer appears.
A language model that works in a loop, choosing actions, seeing their results and deciding the next step until a goal is met.
A model replying with a structured request to run a named action, which the application then executes and reports back.
The repeating cycle of decide, act, observe and decide again that an AI agent follows.
A workflow follows steps a developer fixed in advance; an agent lets the model choose its own steps and tools.
An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources, often likened to a USB-C port for AI.
Several AI agents splitting one task, usually a lead agent handing pieces to helper agents that work in parallel.
Giving an AI agent more tools, permissions or freedom than its task needs, so a mistake or attack causes real damage.
A check outside an AI model that limits what it sees, says or does, such as an input filter or approval step.
A confident AI answer that is false or made up; standards bodies also call it confabulation.
Hidden instructions in a message, web page or file that hijack what an AI model does.
A message crafted to trick an AI model into ignoring its safety rules.
Automatically scoring text or images for harmful content, such as hate or violence, so it can be flagged or blocked.
A person who must review or approve certain AI actions, usually costly or irreversible ones, before they happen.
Tying an AI answer to trusted sources it can quote, so unsupported claims can be caught and removed.
